report:
**Conclusion:** The claim that ibuprofen worsens COVID-19 is not supported by current evidence. It originated from a March 2020 tweet by France’s health minister and a theoretical hypothesis about ACE2 receptor upregulation, but subsequent studies and major health authorities found no link between ibuprofen use and worse COVID-19 outcomes.

**Origin of the claim:** In March 2020, French Health Minister Olivier Véran tweeted that anti-inflammatories like ibuprofen could be “an aggravating factor” in COVID-19 and recommended paracetamol instead. The concern was also fueled by a letter hypothesizing that NSAIDs might upregulate ACE2 receptors (the SARS-CoV-2 entry point), potentially increasing infection risk. However, this was a theoretical mechanism, not clinical proof (https://www.wired.com/story/the-ibuprofen-debate-reveals-the-danger-of-covid-19-rumors/).

**Official guidance:** The World Health Organization clarified that there is no evidence ibuprofen worsens COVID-19 (https://www.cbc.ca/news/health/ibuprofen-covid-19-novel-coronavirus-1.5501496). The U.S. FDA similarly stated it is “not aware of scientific evidence connecting the use of NSAIDs, like ibuprofen, with worsening COVID-19 symptoms” (https://www.fda.gov/drugs/drug-alerts-and-statements/fda-advises-patients-use-non-steroidal-anti-inflammatory-drugs-nsaids-covid-19).

**Research evidence:** A nationwide study found no significant association between ibuprofen prescriptions and severe COVID-19 outcomes (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7537121/). A 2023 narrative review concluded that NSAIDs do not increase susceptibility to infection or worsen COVID-19 outcomes. Observational studies have generally found no increased risk, and some even suggested reduced risk.

**Bottom line:** Your sister’s concern is understandable given the early controversy, but the best available evidence indicates ibuprofen does not worsen COVID-19. Patients should follow their clinician’s advice, but there is no need to avoid ibuprofen out of fear of worsening infection.
